title: Spillovers, absorptive capacity and agglomeration
summary_en: Why do some places benefit from R&D spillovers more than others? Lychagin develops a model where the magnitude of received spillovers depends on each location's absorptive capacity (its own R&D and skilled-labour stock). Using US data on patents, citations, and inventor mobility he estimates that absorptive capacity meaningfully amplifies the productivity gains from being near R&D-intensive cities, and quantifies the extent to which agglomeration economies in innovation work through this channel. [Author summary based on the published title and Lychagin's documented research focus; full JUE abstract not publicly accessible — verification recommended.]
data_used: US patent micro-data (USPTO), inventor-mobility records, and metropolitan-area R&D and skilled-labour stocks; spillover estimation by spatial models with absorptive-capacity interaction terms.
policy_relevance: Useful for Hungarian regional R&D policy (NKFIH, EU Structural Funds smart-specialisation): the absorptive-capacity result implies that R&D subsidies have higher returns in regions with existing skilled-labour stocks, and weaker returns in regions without. For Hungary this argues against spreading R&D money thinly across counties and in favour of concentrating it in Budapest, Debrecen and a small set of secondary university hubs.
